record.title: A paper argues that latent monitors must separate prompt-injection exposure from unsafe-action commitment
record.summary: A paper reports that latent monitors trained on a mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast can flag prompt-injection exposure without reliably predicting which exposed agent will take an unsafe tool action. In a generated-action AgentDojo grid, Qwen's naive contrast gives pre-action AUROC 0.556 for NLA text and 0.672 for an activation probe; training on exposed cases only raises the activation probe to 0.853, close to a matched visible-text TF-IDF baseline at 0.855. The paper reports related commitment-contrast results on Mistral-7B and OLMo-2-7B, but all three model families use AgentDojo and the generated-action study is not a live rollout.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: arXiv records version 1 of the paper as submitted on 12 October 2026 and identifies it as accepted as a poster at the 2026 Agents in the Wild workshop.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a 280-case AgentDojo workspace grid generated by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the paper reports that naive unsafe-versus-rest training predicts pre-action unsafe-tool commitment weakly (activation-probe AUROC 0.672; NLA-text AUROC 0.556), while a commitment-specific contrast raises activation-probe AUROC to 0.853. The trained visible-text TF-IDF baseline reaches 0.855 on the same in-distribution task split.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The author reports commitment-contrast activation-probe AUROC of 0.896 for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and 0.912 for OLMo-2-7B-Instruct on AgentDojo-derived grids, with text baselines at 0.945 and 0.921 respectively. These remain single-paper results on the same benchmark family.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish live-rollout prevention, robustness to adaptive attackers, transferable production thresholds, acceptable clean-traffic false-alarm costs, or independent reproduction of the reported monitor results.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper's reported contrast effect and AUROCs have not been independently reproduced; public artifacts are linked but not audited here.
No live environment rollouts, adaptive attacks, frontier API models, calibrated deployment thresholds, or clean-traffic false-alarm costs were measured.
All three model families are evaluated on AgentDojo-derived grids; external benchmark transfer is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported contrast effect generalizes, it changes how researchers design and interpret latent monitors for unsafe actions in tool-using agents. The results are bounded to one benchmark and small open models, so they do not establish a production safety capability.
limitations: The generated-action experiment is explicitly not a live rollout; labels are based on the model's first generated tool call and inferred unsafe-tool sets.
All three model families use AgentDojo-derived tasks, so cross-model results do not establish benchmark-independent transfer.
Held-out template and suite transfer include only 33 and 15 unsafe positives, respectively; the paper calls these results suggestive.
The strongest in-distribution visible-text TF-IDF baseline matches the logistic activation probe, and the paper reports weak transfer for some probes.
The paper reports that monitors trained on the mixed contrast flag all attacked-but-safe cases and, at the selected threshold, 18 of 40 clean cases for the Qwen activation probe.
Adaptive attackers, deployment thresholds, production API models, and clean-traffic false-alarm costs are not evaluated.
No independent reproduction, artifact audit, or code execution was performed in this activation.

A cited prior paper, arXiv:2606.30449v1, reports scoped negative results across Qwen, Llama and Gemma probe families. Its tasks, models and target labels differ from this paper’s AgentDojo exposure-conditioned contrast; the comparison does not validate or refute the proposed mechanism directly.
brief.summary: A paper reports that latent monitors trained on a mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast can flag prompt-injection exposure without reliably predicting which exposed agent will take an unsafe tool action. In a generated-action AgentDojo grid, Qwen's naive contrast gives pre-action AUROC 0.556 for NLA text and 0.672 for an activation probe; training on exposed cases only raises the activation probe to 0.853, close to a matched visible-text TF-IDF baseline at 0.855. The paper reports related commitment-contrast results on Mistral-7B and OLMo-2-7B, but all three model families use AgentDojo and the generated-action study is not a live rollout.

technical.claimed_result: For a 280-case generated-action AgentDojo workspace grid, the paper reports weak pre-action commitment prediction from the naive mixed contrast (activation AUROC 0.672, NLA-text 0.556) and higher results after commitment-contrast training (activation 0.853, matched visible-text TF-IDF 0.855). It reports a similar conditional signal for activation probes on Mistral-7B and OLMo-2-7B.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary source and its stated v1 date are accessible. The reported AUROCs and behavior are author claims; this activation inspected the paper and repository overview but did not execute code, audit data, or independently reproduce results.
technical.mechanism: The paper separates injection exposure (attacker-controlled content present) from commitment (the model's own subsequent unsafe tool action), both as evaluated labels and training contrasts. It argues that unsafe-versus-rest negatives mix attacked-but-safe with clean cases, so a probe may learn exposure instead of commitment. Restricting training to exposed cases tests prediction of commitment conditional on exposure.
technical.novelty: The double-stratification protocol separates exposure recognition from prediction of an unsafe action and reveals that the naive contrast can learn different axes across model populations. It is an evaluation protocol and bounded paper result, not a deployed defense.
technical.regime: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generated tool choices on AgentDojo-derived workspace tasks; activations from one L40S and one layer-20 NLA verbalizer. Activation-only replication uses Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and OLMo-2-7B-Instruct at matched-relative layer 23. All three model families share the same benchmark family; these are generated benchmark trajectories, not live environment rollouts.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links source code, manifests, exports and outputs; the repository overview lists tests and a deterministic mock harness. No artifact was downloaded, executed or independently audited in this review. A cited negative-results paper was inspected for context; its different tasks and labels make the cross-paper comparison non-equivalent, not an independent reproduction.
technical.strongest_baseline: On Qwen's in-distribution commitment task, a matched visible-text TF-IDF logistic baseline reaches AUROC 0.855 versus 0.853 for the logistic activation probe. Under user-task-grouped folds, the corresponding means are 0.780 and 0.795. Held-out transfer results are based on only 33 and 15 positive cases and do not establish stable cross-population ranking.

brief.title: A paper argues that latent monitors must separate prompt-injection exposure from unsafe-action commitment
brief.why_it_matters: If the contrast effect replicates, a detector validated only on attacked-versus-clean examples may learn to recognize exposure rather than predict unsafe actions. Double-stratifying evaluation and training populations can distinguish those signals and limit misleading monitor claims; the paper does not establish an effective production defense.
